A United Boeing 737-8 MAX, registration N37313 performing flight UA-1207 from Newark,NJ to Jacksonville,FL (USA) with 145 people on board, was climbing through 3000 feet out of runway 22R when the crew advised they had struck a bird on departure, were checking their options and requested delay vectors. The crew consulted with their operations center and returned to Newark for a safe landing on runway 22L about 20 minutes after departure. The crew reported a cracked windshield and a possible pressurization issue. The Boeing 737 MAX 8 was headed to Jacksonville International Airport. The FAA will investigate. A small dent was also found on the right side of the horizontal stabilizer. Impact locations:  #2 engine (ingested), outer edge of #1 engine cowling (possibly some engine ingestion), leading edge of the wing between the fuselage and the #1 engine, horizontal stabilizer.  Based on impact locations, the strike likely involved a minimum of 3-4 birds.  Snarge was not available from the #2 engine.  Four snarge samples collected were collected from #1 Engine (pilot's side). Point 1 - 9 oclock inlet  Point 2 - Inbound inlet ID Point 3 - Fan Blade mid-span shroud  Point 4 - Out board fan low inlet  0826 - 4 FT PIECE OF PLANE Engine FOUND IN NORTH BOUND TURNPIKE MAINTENANCE YARD by PAPD AND NJ State Police. 3/3/25 update:  The strike was captured on airport cameras.  The exact time of the strike was 07:58:43.  Flight data shows the AC at 787 ft at 07:58:44.  The AGL of this strike would be approximately 750 ft AGL. Remains collected from the southeastern edge of the airfield included: 1 wingless/headless Canada goose with a complete neck, the head/neck/left wing of a Canada goose (all attached),  a right wing of a Canada goose (this wing does not seem to match up to the wingless carcass and there is not enough there to match it up to the head/neck/left wing bird), a chunk of breast feathers, 1 injured and completely intact Canada goose that was euthanized.  Samples from all the remains were sent to the SI for confirmation. Impacts to other flights.  Several flights were delayed as a result of this incident - including  JZA872 arrival was delayed 42 minutes, UAL2014 arrival was delayed 1hr and 3 minutes, NKS210 was delayed 18 minutes. CHARM4 airtaxi helicopter called attempting to reach Teterboro Tower (119.5), but they were bleeding over onto KCDW LC. It appears they were unable to hear either CDW or TEB, and appeared to report a bird strike in the middle of their broken transmissions. We coordinated with TEB to relay this information, and eventually the helo started to transition through TEBs airspace. Around this time the chief pilot of CHARM called the landline to relay that he spoke to CHARM4s pilot over the phone and learned the bird strike took out their antenna, but that the aircraft was not experiencing any mechanical issues and would be returning to land at CDW. As CHARM4 approached CDW airspace, radio communications were reestablished. and the aircraft landed without incident.

REMARKS: N703SA, CRJ2, REPORTS THEY EXPERIENCED A BIRD STRIKE ON 8 MILE FINAL FOR RWY 6 AT 1500 FEET. NEGATIVE DAMAGE REPORTED AT THIS TIME, ACN. NOTE: OWNER/ OPERATOR= C&S CRJ200-1 LLC.

We landed at KTTN, runway 06, at about 2120L on August 29, 2024 in Falcon 7X - N347BD.  I was the flying pilot and PIC.  We touched down and just prior to nosewheel touchdown I saw the bird come across the path of the aircraft.  We heard the impact and it looked to have hit the upper part of the nose below the left windshield.  I continued the rollout with no issues.  After shutdown and escorting passengers I call TTN ground control to inform them of the bird strike.  They informed me that they would advise airport ops to search for FOD.  I then went out to post flight and inspect for any damage.  Using a flashlight I thoroughly inspected the entire radome, nose cone and windshields and saw no evidence of any impact.  I continued to inspect the nose gear, main gear, all leading edges and engine turbine blades, nacelles and intakes.  No evidence of any impact was noticed.  After the inspection I spoke with my crewmember and I made the decision to continue our flight which was an empty leg returning to our home base in KMMU.  Prior to engine start the KTTN Fire/Airport Ops vehicle arrived to take information and fill out a wildlife strike form.  They stated to me that they had found the bird intact on the runway.  They looked for evidence to collect from the nose but did not see any.  We then departed to KMMU.  Upon arrival at home base I informed our maintenance team in order to do a follow up inspection.  Our technician inspected the entire aircraft and found no damage.  Inside our hangar with better lighting we did see some residue on the left windshield and no damage. Our right-hand inboard slat sustained a softball-sized dent. BAKERS MF LLC. TWO PHOTOS.  email update from reporter on 4.18.23: sending remains to SI for ID. Destination was KTEB. TWY108. Additional remarks from reporter via email on 4.25.23: On Saturday, April 15, 2023 at approximately 0325Z (Friday, April 14 at 2325L), my co-captain and I experienced a bird strike while approaching KTEB (Teterboro, NJ). I was acting as Pilot in Command (PIC) and Pilot Flying (PF), while my co-captain acted as Second in Command (SIC) and Pilot Monitoring (PM).  We departed CYYZ (Lester B. Pearson Airport, Toronto, Canada) in our Falcon 900EX EASy under Instrument Flight Rules at 0239Z (2239L) on a Part 91 empty repositioning flight to KTEB (Teterboro, NJ).  As we neared the New York terminal area, Approach Control advised us to expect the RNAV (GPS) X Rwy 19 approach. While level at 3,000 feet and roughly 30nm northwest of TEB, the controller instructed us to proceed directly to CUROK, which is the IAF for that approach. Conditions were Night VMC with visibility greater than 10 miles. All of our aircraft’s exterior lights were on.  At about 2325L, while approximately 10 miles northwest of CUROK at 3,000 feet and 250 KIAS, my co-captain and I simultaneously witnessed a small object illuminated by our landing lights on the lower-right side of the aircraft’s nose. There was an audible “thump” associated with it, and we both agreed that we hit something.  The aircraft continued operating normally, and we landed uneventfully at TEB about ten minutes later. However, post-flight inspection revealed a softball-sized dent in the right-hand inboard slat, along with grey feathers and other biological matter extending outboard for at least six feet along the slat. Evidence of bodily fluid splatter was also found on the nacelle of the #3 engine.  We grounded the aircraft pending repair of the damaged slat and inspection of the #3 engine for possible foreign object ingestion.

NOT A STRIKE BUT HAD A NEGATIVE EFFECT ON FLIGHT. NTSB Accident Number: ERA22LA208. SMITH GLORIA M The private pilot was executing a 180° turn at the approach end of the runway to begin takeoff  when she saw a goose crossing the runway near her position. To avoid the goose she relaxed  the turn, and the right main landing gear wheel rolled off the asphalt in an area with a 4-inch  lip. The airplane then rolled down an embankment resulting in substantial damage to the right  wing. The pilot reported that there were no mechanical malfunctions or failures of the airplane  that would have precluded normal operation. Probable Cause and Findings The National Transportation Safety Board determines the probable cause(s) of this accident to be: The pilot’s failure to maintain clearance with the edge of the asphalt, which resulted in a  runway excursion. Contributing to the accident was the pilot’s distraction due to a goose. The goose was the initiating factor that caused the substantial damage to wing, but the goose did not directly cause the damage.
COMMENTS: NOT A STRIKE BUT HAD A NEGATIVE EFFECT ON FLIGHT.

REMARKS: Report from flight crew: We discovered evidence of wildlife/bird strike upon our return to PSM last night. During post flight walk around we noticed blood spatter on the pilot's side of the empennage, just forward of the cargo and on the cargo door. Nothing was there during our preflight in BED earlier that evening, nor on the post/preflight in TEB after dropping off our passenger before heading back to PSM. My FO said he thought he might have noticed something flash in his vision of the left side during departure out of TEB. I did not notice any objects or obstructions in my field of view during our night time departure. During takeoff, and for the rest of the flight no engine/aircraft abnormalities occurred. Upon discovery of the fuselage blood stains I notified maintenance control. Shortly after that two techs came to look at the plane, and they discovered bird impact evidence along the inboard pilots side (left) wing leading edge. No other debris was noticeable to us in the wheel wells, landing gear, engine area, or other areas typically associated with bird strike damage. Safety Department Comment: Maintenance inspection showed no damage.  Aircraft time out of service longer than normal because incident took place late in the evening and the aircraft was not scheduled to fly until late the next day.
